LOHRA Order 06/03/2017 Petitioner has laid this criminal misc. petition under Section 482 Cr.P.C. to assail order of cognizance for offence under Section 193 IPC passed by Metropolitan Magistrate No.3,
Jodhpur Metropolitan (for short, 'learned trial Court') and affirmed by Additional District and Sessions Judge No.3, Jodhpur Metropolitan (for short, 'learned revisional Court').

entities.text: Additional District and Sessions Judge No.3, Jodhpur Metropolitan
entities.label: COURT

sentences.text: The facts, in brief, giving rise to this petition are that in the year 1999, petitioner was working as Chief Medical and Health Officer, Jodhpur and as such was empowered to give written consent and authorize someone to launch prosecution by resorting to Section 20 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 (for short, 'Act of 1954') (since repealed).

It so happened that Food Inspector was Om Prakash Kalla took sample of Mustard Oil on (2 of 6) [CRLMP-778/2015] 25.09.1999,
which after analysis was found adulterated.

After completion of the entire process, the matter was placed before the petitioner for his written consent to file complaint against the accused person for offence punishable under Section 7/16 of the Act of 1954.
During trial, Om Prakash Kalla appeared in the witness-box and the petitioner examined as a prosecution witness besides other witnesses.

Learned trial Court, on conclusion of trial, acquitted the accused but, taking into account some contradictions in the statements of petitioner as well as Om Prakash Kalla, directed the Assistant Public Prosecutor to file complaint against petitioner and Om Prakash Kalla for filing wrong complaint and giving contradictory statements in the Court.

Pursuant to the directions of the Court,
Assistant Public Prosecutor filed a complaint against the petitioner and Om Prakash Kalla under Section 193 IPC read with Section 195 and 340 Cr.P.C. before learned trial Court.
The learned trial Court, by its order dated 15.03.2013, took cognizance against the petitioner and other incumbent Om Prakash Kalla for offence under Section 193 IPC.

sentences.text: Being aggrieved by the said order, the petitioner filed a revision petition before learned revisional Court but the learned revision Court declined to interfere with the order of cognizance.
Therefore, in that background, petitioner has approached this Court.

Mr. P.N. Mohanani, learned counsel for the petitioner, submits that mere contradictions in the statements of two witnesses cannot constitute offence of perjury within the meaning of Section (3 of 6) [CRLMP-778/2015] 193 IPC.

It is argued by learned counsel that the basic ingredient for constituting offence of perjury is deliberate and conscious attempt by an individual to give false statements or to file false affidavit before the Court.

Learned counsel for the petitioner would contend that role of the petitioner was limited to the extent of giving written consent or authorizing a person to file complaint and, therefore, even considering the limited role of the petitioner under Section 20 of the Act of 1954, he cannot be prosecuted for offence under Section 193 IPC.

In substance, submission of the learned counsel is that order of cognizance by the learned trial Court and its affirmation by the learned revisional Court is per se vulnerable and cannot be sustained.
In support of his contention, learned counsel has placed reliance on a decision of Supreme Court in Ashok Kuamr Aggarwal Vs. Union of India & Ors.:2014 Cri.L.J. 1213.

entities.text: Ashok Kuamr Aggarwal Vs. Union of India & Ors.:2014 Cri.L.J. 1213
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Per contra, learned Public Prosecutor has vehemently opposed the petition and has urged that the order of cognizance passed by learned trial Court has been affirmed by revisional Court, therefore, it is not desirable to exercise second power of judicial review in the matter.

Learned Public Prosecutor has further submitted that serious contradictions in the statements of petitioner and Om Prakash Kalla have rightly persuaded the learned trial Court to order prosecution of the petitioner and other incumbent for offence of perjury while passing the verdict of acquittal.
[CRLMP-778/2015] I have heard learned counsel for the petitioner as well as learned Public Prosecutor, perused the impugned order and the entire record of the case.
It is not in dispute that sample of Mustard Oil was collected by Food Inspector Om Prakash Kalla and got analysed from Laboratory.

Subsequently, when in the report it was revealed that oil is adulterated, at his behest, endeavour was made for seeking consent of the petitioner and sanction for authorizing someone to lay complaint in the matter.

Therefore, the exercise of collecting sample and getting it analysed from analyst was undertaken by Food Inspector and it was only after that exercise petitioner's consent was sought for laying complaint in the matter.

In these circumstances,
it is rather difficult to comprehend that petitioner was directly involved in false prosecution of the accused for offence punishable under Section 7/16 of the Act of 1954.
It is also noteworthy that mere contradictions in the statements of the witnesses itself cannot constitute an offence of perjury.

There cannot be two opinions that offence of perjury is a very serious offence but looking to the seriousness of offence strict proof is also required so as to launch prosecution against an individual.

Indisputably, the Court which orders for prosecution of an individual for perjury is required to see whether there was any deliberate or conscious attempt by someone to make false deposition on oath or tendering a false affidavit in the Court.
Moreover, it is also necessary that the incumbent, who is sought (5 of 6) [CRLMP-778/2015] to be charged for perjury, has made an attempt to mislead the Court.

At this juncture, it is also desirable to examine Dr.Santosh Singh vs State on 6 March, 2017 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/122661242/
2 expediency for initiating criminal proceedings against the petitioner for perjury.

sentences.text: Provisions contained in Section 340 Cr.P.C. are alluded only for the purpose of showing that necessary care and caution are to be taken before initiating a criminal proceeding for perjury against the deponent of contradictory statements in a judicial proceedings.
Thus, taking into account the factual backdrop of the instant case, I am afraid, the learned trial Court has not cared to examine true purport and rigor of Section 340 Cr.P.C.

In totality, after examining offence under Section 193 IPC in conjunction with the role of the petitioner under Section 20 of the Act of 1954, I am convinced that per se prosecution of the petitioner under Section 193 IPC is unsustainable which ipso facto makes the impugned order of cognizance, affirmed by the learned revisional Court, vulnerable.
Reliance in this behalf can be profitably made to the case of Ashok Kumar Aggarwal (supra), on which, learned counsel for the petitioner has placed reliance.

In this verdict, the Supreme Court, while considering the provisions of Sections 195 and 340 Cr.P.C., has held:
"12.

The High Court while dealing with the case has also, after examining the original records as well as the file and particularly the confidential notings therein, came to the conclusion that in view of the directions issued by the superior authority, some other witnesses were examined "to tighten the loose ends of the case" and there was no attempt on the part of the investigating agency to mislead the court.
The order dated 23.4.2002 passed by the Director, CBI has not been challenged by the appellant and the instant complaint had been filed after 3-1/2 years in 2006.

The statements were recorded on such directions, however, only to the extent of (6 of 6)
[CRLMP-778/2015] tightening the loose ends.
More so, the provisions of Section 195(1)(b) etc. are also attracted in such a fact-situation.
After looking into the voluminous record of the case, what has been done after filing the affidavit or making the statement was minimal.

The prosecution for perjury is required only where perjury appears to be deliberate and conscious and the conviction is reasonable,
probable or likely.
In the circumstances, a mere impression or perception of the appellant would not make the deposition on affidavit by the respondent no. 5 to be false as being a deliberate and conscious act.

13. The court further observed that the complaint had been filed after 4 years on the basis of mere impression of the appellant and under no circumstances, it could be held that there had been some deliberate and conscious attempt to mislead the court which may warrant entertaining the application filed by the appellant."
In view of foregoing discussion, I feel persuaded to accept this petition.

Accordingly, the same is allowed and the impugned order of cognizance, passed by the learned trial Court, and order passed by the learned revision Court affirming the same, are hereby quashed and set aside qua the petitioner.
(P.K. LOHRA)J. Bharti/1
